Thanks for your comments Adrian.

Going back to Sarah's question about segment size relative to covariate resolution (I take it that is what 'pixel' was referencing).

This is a philosophical problem, but one that deserves thought.  The concept is to model the animals' relationship with their environment.  But easier said than done.  Sampling of the animals is being done via the transect survey whereas sampling of the environment is being done by different researchers (from outer space).  In a perfect world, those two investigations would be conducted at the same scale, but this is life as we know it.

Sarah's suggestion of re-segmenting such that the animal sampling is 'scaled up' to the more coarse environment sampling is probably a sound choice.

messages.body_plain:
Hi,
This post seems to conflate a number of issues, and I’m not clear which is the biggest problem.  If the issue is over dispersion (e.g., if the vast majority of short segments contain zero sightings), it’d be worth trying a Tweedie distribution in addition to trying longer segments.  That helped in two of our studies that had a lot of zeroes:
http://www.nature.com/articles/srep04170
http://digitalcommons.unl.edu/cgi/viewcontent.cgi?article=1328&context=usdeptcommercepub

If there are many sightings, most segments contain sightings, and the poor fit is due to variability in environmental conditions along long segments, or lack of variability in environmental conditions among short segments, that’s a different problem with a different solution.  If it’s a tiny study area, maybe environmental conditions didn’t vary much throughout the survey region, and you need more informative covariates.  Maybe that’s poor model fit is the answer — variability in X across the range of values of X you observed, doesn’t explain much variability in encounter rate.

Choice of segment length was raised as a priority area for future research in Hedley’s original thesis: http://www.creem.st-and.ac.uk/sharon/public_html/thesis.pdf  Hedley recommended checking how sensitive your model fit is to choice of segment length. If segment length is causing your answers to vary by a lot, is it worth choosing one of Hedley’s other methods, such as the waiting distances method, which is less reliant than the count method on choice of segment length?  Adrian raises a good point:  density surface models relax a lot of assumptions about sampling design, but they still assume reasonable coverage across the range of all covariates in the model.  If that assumption was violated, I could imagine poor fit and wild extrapolations.

I think a bit more detail is needed to narrow down the laundry list of potential explanations, so people can offer more helpful advice.

All the best,
Rob

messages.body_plain:
The Centre for Research into Ecological and Environmental Modelling (CREEM) is hosting two linked workshops in the summer of 2016 in our purpose-built facilities at the University of St. Andrews, Scotland. Participation in these workshops will train participants in the latest methods for design and analysis of distance sampling surveys, including line and point transects. The workshops are taught by leading researchers in the field, using industry-standard software.

The first workshop (16-19 August) will run at an introductory level, and will focus on distance sampling methods, largely described in the standard reference book "Introduction to Distance Sampling." The workshop will be a blend of theory and practice and participants will learn how to use the program "Distance." Participants will gain a solid grounding in both survey design and methods of analysis for distance sampling surveys.  Note that we have moved the 'automated survey design' and 'incorporating covariates in detection function' from the advanced workshop into the introductory workshop.

The advanced distance sampling workshop (22-25 August) will include advanced treatment of analyses in which detectability on the transect line is not assumed to be perfect (the so-called g(0) problem) and spatial (or density surface) modelling. We will showcase a series of R packages for performing standard as well as sophisticated analyses in R. The aim of this workshop is to perform non-standard and sophisticated distance sampling analyses. It is also an opportunity for those actively engaged in the design, analysis and execution of distance sampling surveys to discuss common issues and problems, and set future research directions. The workshop will be a combination of lectures and computer sessions, with considerable time for discussion.

For all workshops, participants are encouraged to bring their own data sets, and can expect to do some preliminary analyses with their data.  Computer sessions take place in our modern computer classroom (attached to the seminar room); participants can use our computers or bring their own laptops.

Additional details regarding the workshop can be found at our website

Hello All,

Originally my segments were around 4 m each (due to small ESW). This was leading to around 50,000 segments and a lot of segment centroids on the same pixel (30m spatial resolution for covariates). I tested a segment size of 30 m and a segment size of 90 m and found that the models, negative binomial and tweedie both performed better (higher AIC and more deviance explained) than the original 4m or 30m segments. I also tested dividing up my study area and found that by focusing on either half of the study area, I increased deviance explained by 50%. So, Adrian is correct in that maybe my segments (when modeled over the entire study area) are not covering the full range of the covariates used in the model. However, I do recommend paying attention to the spatial scale of covariates when determining segment length!  I went from around 8% deviance explained to 20-25% deviance explained by increasing segment size.

Peace, Sarah

If the issue is over dispersion (e.g., if the vast majority of short segments contain zero sightings), it’d be worth trying a Tweedie distribution in addition to trying longer segments. Maybe that’s poor model fit is the answer — variability in X across the range of values of X you observed, doesn’t explain much variability in encounter rate.

If segment length is causing your answers to vary by a lot, is it worth choosing one of Hedley’s other methods, such as the waiting distances method, which is less reliant than the count method on choice of segment length?  Adrian raises a good point:  density surface models relax a lot of assumptions about sampling design, but they still assume reasonable coverage across the range of all covariates in the model.  If that assumption was violated, I could imagine poor fit and wild extrapolations.

standard approach will probably work OK, provided the detection functions
for different cue types are not too extreme.  You could try analyses with
and without cue type as a factor to check this.

Guillaume,

I recently encountered a similar challenge where I wanted to re-create my own detection function plots in R.

You might want to inspect the mrds:::detfct function, and extract the code that is relevant to your example.
I think your issue may (in part at least) be due to a lack of scaling of the detection function.

Below is a short script I put together to plot a hazard-rate model with one factor variable.
It did not (admittedly) include an expansion series, but it should hopefully put you on the right track (especially if you look at mrds:::detfct).

# Scaling factor needed for correct plotting
# From mrds:::scalevalue
scale.value<-function (key.scale, z)
{exp(as.matrix(z) %*% key.scale)}

# This function calculates the detection probability according to a hazard rate model
# from mrds:::keyfct.hz
key.fct.hz<-function (distance, key.scale, key.shape)
{ return(1 - exp(-(distance/key.scale)^(-key.shape)))}

# Vector of distances used to re-create the detection function (from 0 out to truncation distance of 250 m)
distances<-seq(0,250,length.out = 100)

# Using a hazard-rate model with one (dichotomous, 1/0) factor variable that only affects the scale
# (not the shape) of the detection function:

# Shape parameter
key.shape<-scale.value(model$ddf$ds$aux$ddfobj$shape$parameters,
                       matrix(1,nrow = 100,1))

# Scale parameter
# Factor = 0
mat0<-matrix(1,nrow = 100,ncol = 2)
mat0[,2]<-0
key.scale0<-scale.value(model$ddf$ds$aux$ddfobj$scale$parameters,mat0)

# Factor = 1
mat1<-matrix(1,nrow = 100,ncol = 2)
key.scale1<-scale.value(model$ddf$ds$aux$ddfobj$scale$parameters,mat1)

# Calculate detection probability values
y.val0<- key.fct.hz(distances, key.scale0, key.shape)
y.val1<- key.fct.hz(distances, key.scale1, key.shape)

# Now let's re-create the histogram
# from mrds:::detfct
bindata <- function(x, r, breaks) {
  return(hist(r[r >= x[1] & r <= x[2]], breaks = breaks,
              plot = FALSE)$counts)}
sumit <- function(x, n, wt) {
  return(sum(x/(wt * n)))}
selected <- rep(TRUE, nrow(model$ddf$ds$aux$ddfobj$xmat))

# Detection probability for each fitted value & Nhat estimate
if (length(model$ddf$fitted) == 1) {
  pdot <- rep(model$ddf$fitted, sum(as.numeric(selected)))
}else {
  pdot <- model$ddf$fitted[selected]
  Nhat <- sum(1/pdot)
}

# Create a dummy histogram (h1)
# dist.data is the data.frame object of the distance data
# Right-truncating here at 250 m
# If you inspect the internal functions of the mrds package, you will find how the number of histogram breaks is calculated. In my case, the value is 11
h1<-hist(dist.data[dist.data$distance<=250,]$distance, breaks=seq(0,250,250/11))

# Calculate expected counts for each distance value
expected.counts <- apply(t(as.matrix(c(0,250))), 1, bindata, r = (0:1000) * 250/1001, breaks = seq(0,250,250/11))
expected.counts <- apply(expected.counts, 1, sumit, n = 1001, wt = pdot)

# Re-scale the counts
h1$counts<-h1$counts/expected.counts

# Use the ggplot2 package to plot the histogram (as rectangles) and overlay the detection function
# plotting options
gg.opts <- theme(panel.grid.major=element_blank(),
                 panel.grid.minor=element_blank(),

Hi Phil,

Thanks for your answer. It seems to be one of the clues for my problem.
Indeed, I have always the feeling that something is not exactly on the right scale ...

First, I solved aprt of my problem: I had looked at the mrds function to see how the expansion series were built. I found that the function returns the exp(adj.series) to ensure that g(y)>0.
> mrds:::adjfct.herm

adjfct.herm <-
       function(distance,scaling=1,adj.order,adj.parm=NULL,adj.exp=FALSE)
#
# adjfct.herm
#
# Hermite polynomial adjustment terms
#
#
# Arguments:
#
# distance  - perpendicular distance vector
# scaling     - scale parameter
# adj.order - vector of orders of polynomials to fit
# adj.parm  - vector of parameters (a_j)
#
{
# Check the adjustment parameters
 if(is.null(adj.parm)){
         adj.parm <- as.vector(rep(1,length(adj.order)))
}

        adj.order <- as.vector(adj.order)

        hermsum <- 0

       for(i in 1:length(adj.order))

#   if adj.exp return exp(hermsum) to keep f(x)>0
        if(adj.exp)
            return(exp(hermsum))
   else
           return(hermsum)
}

messages.body_plain:
Fabrice

Welcome.  First correspondent, to my knowledge, from the Reunion Island.

There are a couple of layers in my answer to your question.  If I think
only about size of burrow, I would probably measure that as a
'continuous' variable in the field.  However, you note that you have a
column in your Distance data named 'species'.  From this, I presume you
have transformed your burrow size measurements into 'species', hence
have converted your 'continuous' variable into a 'factor' or discrete
variable.

Assuming this is the case (species is a factor--taking on 1 of a small
number of categories), you can produce "species-specific" estimates of
burrow density in two ways.

Post-stratify your analysis by "species" (see the section
"Stratification and post-stratification" in the Conventional Distance
Sampling chapter), this will cause Distance to produce separate
detection functions (and density estimates) for each burrow type.

You can then choose to either fit separate detection functions for each
burrow size (this carries the assumption that burrows from different
species have different detectabilities, this should work well if you
have sufficient detections for each 'species' of burrow), or pool
detections across species (if there are some species for which there are
few detected burrows; however this carries the danger of using the
'wrong' detection function for each of the species types, this may
induce a bias in the result).

Alternatively you can use the MCDS engine to use burrow size as a
covariate in the detection function (a half-way house between the
previous two options, using the MCDS engine).

If you are interested in the overall burrow density (independent of
species), you would look at the sum of the size-specific estimates.

This issue has been sorted. In the end I used a detection function created in the R package Distance and ditched the dummy ddf. The dummy ddf I was using did not have detection function uncertainty associated with it that "dsm.var.gam" was looking for. This error was caused when the predicted abundance for each grid cell was too high (awful model!) and R replaced the predicted value with "Inf". "Inf" is short for Infinity!

Thank you kindly to David Miller for helping me out of this bother!

Greg Lollback

We are talking past each other a bit.  I understand you wish to draft your figure from first principles. library(Distance)

mrds:::plot.ds(ddf.hour.hn <http://ddf.hour.hn>$ddf,pdf=TRUE)

With HAS==Hour after Sunrise serving as a factor covariate, the shape of the detection function at different levels of this covariate are apparent in the resulting PDF:

Complicated question, with many possible answers.

Do you believe the detection function changes each year, do you believe the cluster size dynamics changes each year; do you believe the relationship of animal location and environmental covariates change each year?  If yes, then the flippant answer is to fit separate detection functions and spatial models to each years' data.  That approach is not commonly taken.

At the other extreme, if you believe the detection function, cluster size dynamics and covariate response does not change over the study, then fit a single detection and dsm model.  Build separate prediction grids using the annual values for the environmental covariates, produce annual predictions from the prediction grids, acknowledge the variation in the annual estimates.

There are many more variants of those approaches that could be taken.  Others will doubtless offer you other suggestions.

messages.subject: Electronic inclinometer for distance sampling surveys
messages.subject_clean: Electronic inclinometer for distance sampling surveys
messages.body_plain:
Greetings fellow surveyors,

This summer I led an aerial survey in Icelandic waters. While the survey itself was not a great success (because of weather), I was able to trial a new device, which we have called a "geometer", to measure declination and yaw angles to sightings. The devices performed very well and were a real improvement over the analogue inclinometers we have used in previous surveys.

The geometer was developed by an engineering consultant in Iceland, funded by NAMMCO and the Icelandic Marine Research Institute. The geometer uses 3-D accelerometers, a 3-D gyroscope and a 3-D magnetometer to measure the pitch, roll and yaw of the device, and records these measurements, along with the clock time of the computer, to a text file when a button is depressed. It is also fitted with a "red dot" rifle sight (http://bushnell.com/all-products/rifle-scopes/trophy-red-dot/first-strike) to facilitate aiming. The observer points the device at the sighting by aligning the LED red dot over the sighting, and depresses the button to record the time, declination, yaw and roll angles. The device is connected to a laptop via a USB port (future versions may be wireless), and the associated software allows up to 4 geometers to be run simultaneously on one computer.  Further information on the geometer is available at http://geometer.pitemp.com/ .

I believe the geometer offers a few advantages over conventional analogue and digital inclinometers available commercially:
1. Ease of use. The observer simply aims and presses the button. No requirement to read the often double and difficult scales of conventional inclinometers (e.g. Suunto's);
2. Less opportunity for observer error. We all know that observers make errors reading inclinometers and recording their readings. With the geometer the measurements are recorded automatically at the press of a button.
3. Accurate timing of observations. The exact time (to the second) is recorded every time the button is pressed.
4.  Easier data transcription. The text files produced can be read directly into Excel or other programs.
5. Simultaneous recording of declination and yaw angles, potentially eliminating the need to make measurements only when the sighting comes abeam of the aircraft.

The version of the device I used in Iceland was a prototype, and a new improved version is being developed by a firm in Iceland. As there is likely to be limited demand for a device such as this, the developer is trying to gauge the level of interest among surveyors in purchasing the new version.  You can also communicate directly with the developer to influence what features (e.g. GPS input, voice recording) should be included in the new version.

I should make clear here that I am not financially involved in the project and do not stand to gain by their production and sale. My interest is mainly to make a "better mousetrap" available to those of us in this field (including me). Unfortunately I am pretty sure that the developer will not continue to improve the device unless there is some assurance that he can at least recoup his investment.

Therefore,  I would encourage you to check out the web page at http://geometer.pitemp.com/ and register your interest if you think this device might be something you could use.

Best regards,

Daniel Pike.
Esox Associates

messages.subject: Following tracks in the snow to animals by helicopter- Is distance sampling possible?
messages.subject_clean: Following tracks in the snow to animals by helicopter- Is distance sampling possible?
messages.body_plain:
Hi group,

I am participating in an ungulate aerial survey where methods used in the past have aimed to determine Minimum Animal Counts and included following tracks left in the snow to find groups, determine group size and age/sex ratios.

We are wanting to incorporate distance sampling to properly estimate the portion of the study area we are sampling. Thus, we would fly systematic (random start) line-transects and search for tracks and/or animals. We would then follow the tracks to the animals to determine group size, etc.

A few more survey details:
We will fly at a pre-determined time following a snowfall to have enough, but not too many, tracks. We will fly mid-day on bright days so the tracks are easier to spot. We may incorporate Mark-Recapture Distance Sampling to correct for animals missed on the track line.

I can think of three approaches:

1- Measure distances only to animals that are detected directly from the flight path.

We would not follow tracks to animals as has been done in the past. We would only count, and measure distances to, animals we can physically detect from the flight path.

My concerns with this approach:
-Too few animals will be included in the survey to properly model the detection function and estimate the density.
-We would lose the additional information (e.g. age/sex ratios) gained by finding more groups through following tracks.

2- Measure distance to tracks.

We would measure the distance where the tracks were first spotted. For cluster size, it seems the relationship of larger groups being observable from a larger distance would hold: large groups leave more tracks that are easier to spot from a distance.

My concerns with this approach:
-Is it valid?
-Tracks are often linear on the landscape and it might be difficult to assess which portion of tracks was first spotted to accurately measure distances, particularly for tracks that run perpendicular to the flight path.
-Not all animals will be found by following tracks (i.e. some tracks won't lead to animals).

3- Measure distance to animals, wherever they are found.

We would measure the distance to the actual animals, regardless of whether they were spotted directly or found through following tracks. For cluster size, it seems the relationships of larger groups being observed at larger distances would hold: larger groups leave more tracks, which are easier to follow farther away from the flight path.

My concerns with this approach:
-Is it valid?
-Some groups may be at a significant distance from the flight path, possibly at the next transect.
-Our detection distances might be highly variable, and difficult to model.

Any advice would be appreciated.

Regards,
Natalie.

There are a number of researchers examining snow tracks to measure occupancy (rather than abundance) particularly for animals occurring at low density, e.g. wolverines.  For example, a recent paper
Whittington, J., K. Heuer, B. Hunt, M. Hebblewhite, and P. M. Lukacs. 2015. ‘Estimating Occupancy Using Spatially and Temporally Replicated Snow Surveys: Estimating Occupancy by Snow Surveys’. Animal Conservation 18 (1): 92–101. doi:10.1111/acv.12140.

might get you started into the literature.

Thinking back even further on the subject of wolverines, a couple more papers come to light:

Becker, E. F., H. N. Golden, and C. L. Gardner. 2004. Using probability sampling of animal tracks
in snow to estimate population size. Pages 248–270 inW. L. Thompson, editor. Sampling rare or
elusive species: Concepts, designs, and techniques for estimating population parameters. Island
Press, Washington, D.C.
Becker, E. F., M. A. Spindler, and T. O. Osborne. 1998. A population estimator based on network sampling of tracks in the snow. Journal of Wildlife Management 62:968–977.

As I recall, these methods do not make use of distance sampling, rather cutting of animal tracks by transects, then following tracks back to the animal.

See if these approaches might be suitable to your intended use.

Hello all,

I'm attempting to examine trends in lemur density, both how they are influenced by habitat degradation, and what their trend is over time. For the habitat degradation, I am stratifying by discrete classes (A = intact, B = intermediate, C = degraded), and for the annual trends, I have one site that has 4 years' worth of data, and another site with 3 years' worth of data.

My problem is that it always seems to be the last stratum that has an issue with precision. For example, for the habitat degradation analysis, the degraded site has the fewest lemur observations (around 13). I would assume that estimating density using a strata-specific detection probability would decrease precision, and that's what happens.

However, even when running a global detection probability, where presumably detection is being pooled from all the observations, I still have terrible precision for the degraded site (see attached bar chart).

I could understand that since there are so few observations, but with my examination of annual trends, I'm facing the same problem, when the last year actually has the most observations (32), compared to the other years (see screenshot attached). The first three years, even with less than 30 observations for each year, have perfectly fine precision and confidence intervals, but the last year, with the most observations, has an absolutely horrendous precision estimate.

I don't know what's going on, and I would very much appreciate any help that anyone can give me.

messages.body_plain:
A handful of issues here Asia.

First, precision of density estimates from distance sampling is comprised of two bits:  how uncertain you are about the shape of the detection function, which enlightens you about the confidence you have in the proportion of animals you missed within the region covered by your transects; and variability in animals encountered on you replicate transects.  This second component informs you about confidence you can have extrapolating from transects you visited to the entire study area.

Imagine your replicate transects as boxes of chocolates.  If you open a box 1 and find 12 chocolates, then open box 2 and find 12 and box 3 and find 12, how many chocolates would you guess there to be in each of a stack of boxes you haven't opened?  In contrast if your sample of 3 boxes possessed 25, 3 and 15 chocolates, respectively, how confident are you about the contents of unopened boxes.

I speculate it is this encounter rate variance that is responsible for the poor precision in the degraded habitat and the last year.

I know nothing about lemurs, but if the degradation you describe is patchy, with some of your replicate transects in remnants that have not yet been degraded and other replicates degraded, that may heighten the difference in number of encounters between transects.

Look through the Distance output and find the page labelled "Density Estimates/Global" and at the bottom you will see a table labelled "Component percentages of Var(D)".  This will tell you what piece (detection function/encounter rate/(maybe)cluster size) contributes to the uncertainty in your overall estimates.

Other comments:  using a global detection function to apply to make stratum-specific estimates results in an inappropriate detection function being applied to each stratum, leading to some bias.  If the strata are spatial, that means you are using detections from, say, degraded habitats in your detection function for your intact habitats (and vice versa).  In addition, if your strata are temporal, then applying a single global detection function to produce annual estimates induces dependence between the annual estimates mucking up the precision estimates of the individual estimates.

I suspect you are on the edge with respect to number of detections for fitting your detection function as well as the amount of replicate transects you have.  Hence the uncertainty you have in your estimates are challenging your ability to see clear patterns.
